Testimony in Support of LD 594: "Resolve, Directing the State Auditor to Audit All State Agencies"
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and distinguished members of the Committee on State and Local Government, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony in support of LD 594, "Resolve, Directing the State Auditor to Audit All State Agencies."
The Importance of Transparency and Accountability
LD 594 is a crucial step toward increasing transparency, accountability, and efficiency in Maine state government. By requiring the State Auditor to conduct a comprehensive audit of all state agencies, this legislation ensures that taxpayers and policymakers clearly understand how state resources are allocated and spent.
With the state government's growing size and complexity, the public and the Legislature must have complete oversight of agency operations, staffing levels, budget growth, and project efficiency. Between 2019 and 2025, the biennial budget grew from around 7.2 billion1 to around 10.5 billion,2 a $1.7 billion dollar increase even after adjusting for inflation.3 The Governor's proposed budget increases allocations by another $1.1 billion, and this massive increase in spending should also come with an increase in oversight.4
A comprehensive audit will provide lawmakers with the data necessary to make informed decisions about the effectiveness of agency programs and expenditures.
Benefits of LD 594
- Enhanced Fiscal Responsibility: Auditing all state agencies will identify inefficiency, waste, and potential savings within the state budget. This will enable policymakers to reallocate resources to programs that deliver the highest value to Maine citizens.
- Reducing Wasteful Spending: As shown above, Maine's current budget deficit has correlated with a significant increase in spending, and auditing our

https://www.calculator.net/inflation-calculator.html?cstartingamount1=1&cinmonth1=1&cinyear1=2023&coutmont h1=12&coutyear1=2024&calctype=1&x=Calculate#uscpi 4 https://www.maine.gov/budget/home

state's spending habits would be a practical first step in case Maine needs to perform budgetary triage in the future. - Improved Government Performance: By tracking the scope of completed and incomplete projects, LD 594 will help the Legislature assess agency effectiveness and ensure that taxpayer dollars are used efficiently to promptly complete critical projects. - Workforce Transparency: The resolve's requirement to report the number of current employees, newly hired employees, and overall staffing trends will provide valuable insight into government employment growth and whether staffing levels are aligned with the needs of each agency. - Data-Driven Budgeting: The requirement to analyze each agency's budget growth over time and its share of the total biennial budget will provide lawmakers with an essential tool for assessing long-term spending trends and determining whether budgets should be adjusted. - Strengthened Public Trust: A government that is transparent and accountable to the people it serves fosters greater trust among taxpayers. Regular audits and reporting mechanisms ensure that agencies are operating efficiently and in the public's best interest.
Ensuring Effective Implementation
While LD 594 is a necessary and positive step, we encourage the committee to ensure that the auditing process minimizes disruption to agency operations while still providing a thorough and accurate review. The State Auditor should be granted the resources to complete this audit without delay, and the resulting reports should be made easily accessible to both the public and policymakers.
Conclusion
LD 594 is a common-sense measure that will provide essential oversight of state agencies, ensure responsible fiscal management, and give policymakers the tools they need to make informed budgetary decisions. By passing this resolve, the Legislature will take an important step in promoting good governance, efficiency, and public trust in Maine state government.
For these reasons, we respectfully urge the committee to support LD 594 and advance it for enactment. Thank you for your time and consideration.
186072:
TESTIMONY OF MATT DUNLAP, CIA
MAINE STATE AUDITOR
IN OPPOSITION
LD 594, Resolve, Directing the State Auditor to Audit All State Agencies
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee
on State and Local Govermnent, my name is Matt Dunlap, and I live in Old Town, and am privileged to
serve as State Auditor.
We appreciate the language offered by the sponsor of this legislation; however, we are in opposition to
this bill as written. The general premise behind this bill is not unsound; to gather for the use of the Legislature a compendium and review of information about programs and agencies, including staffing level changes over time and budgetary growth. What the Resolve directs is not an audit, however, but rather a performance review of the type already within the purview of the Office of Program Evaluation and Governmental Accountability to engage in. It is also doubtful that such a one-time review, even over distinct, five-year periods of time, would be of the same utility to lawmakers as the type of year-to-year
comparison available now through materials tracked either by the Office of the State Controller, the
Office of Fiscal and Program Review, or the Single Audit document produced by our office. To provide for that type of timeline comparison, this legislation would have to be considerably redrafted--beyond the
parameters of the parliamentary precedent--to accomplish that end. We believe that in order for the title
of this bill to actually cover both financial and compliance audits of all state agencies over time, it would need to be an Act, and not a Resolve, and as you well know, Resolves cannot be amended to become Acts.
Further, it would require a substantial fiscal note that we have not estimated in order to provide the
_
necessary resources to achieve the end described in the title as we understand it.
While I don't wish to complicate the question further, I will anyway. Even a year-over-year comparison must be viewed with caution, as the nature of government has changed over time; for over a hundred
years, we had no state agencies as we recognize them today; the military was managed by States, not the
Federal govermnent; our taxation bases have changed dramatically from a mix of import duties, state property taxes and poll taxes to primarily a mix of Federal dollars, service fees, and sales and income taxes; and even the nature and value of a dollar has changed through the sundry Coinage and Banking Acts enjoined over the last two hundred years by Congress. It certainly blurs the growth slope in understanding state expenditures from 1820, when the state spent a total of $1,329.91 to somewhere in the neighborhood of $12 billion today.
Under Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards for government audits employed for the audit of the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report and the Single Audit Act, our office conducts audits of
various Federal programs and funds. Taken together, these audits cover over 80% of state expenditures
and 91.5% of Federal programs. Further, under the mantle of our work to audit the state's financial statements, every state agency is subject to that audit. That information is already available.
I am happy to answer any questions of the committee at this time at the pleasure of the chair.

To Members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government
Regarding L.D. 594, "Resolve, Directing the State Auditor to Audit All State Agencies."
March 17, 2025
Sen. Baldacci, Rep. Salisbury, and members of the State and Local Government Committee, thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony before you today. I'm Penny Morrell, taxpayer and citizen of the Town of Belgrade, Maine.
I support L.D. 594, "Resolve, Directing the State Auditor to Audit All State Agencies." I believe this bill is necessary and has been for years. I worked in DHHS for three or more years trying to get to retirement and witnessed firsthand waste, fraud, and abuse of public funds. I also worked for the non-profit, Maine Administrators of Services for Children With Disabilities (MADSEC), and can testify to waste in the Department of Education as well. The media covered the fact that the previous Senate President was paid mileage for trips to his home in Aroostook County that he never made because he was staying in Augusta. He never had to pay back those fraudulent monies he charged us, the State of Maine. That's just one more example of what I'm talking about. With what has been discovered at the Federal level of waste, fraud, and abuse, it only makes sense to audit every department in Maine State Government to gut the waste, fraud, and abuse of taxpayer funds once and for all. I urge this committee to vote "ought to pass" on LD 594. Thank you.

The genesis of this bill came out of a comments from constituents who,
given the growth and increasing complexity of state government, do not have a good understanding or comfort in where their tax dollars are being spent. Current law authorizes the State Auditor to conduct audits of all state government departments and agencies, as well as the accounts and financial records of entities receiving an appropriation or grant from the State of Maine. However, it would instill more confidence and trust of Maine residents ifthe State Auditor were directedto conduct such audits, which would include those items specified in the bill. This would help citizens, as well as Legislators, to better gauge the changes that have occurred over time within each department, including the number of employees and expenditures.
